artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_3 = \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ and consider the elementary abelian group $\mathbb{F}_3^r$ for an integer $r \geq 1$. A subset $A$ of an additively written abelian group $G$ is called sum-free if there are no elements $x,y,z \in A$ with $x+y=z$. A sum-free subset $A \subseteq G$ is called induced if there exists a non-zero subgroup $H \leq G$ such that $A$ is the full preimage under the canonical homomorphism $G \to G/H$ of a sum-free subset of $G/H$; equivalently, $A$ is a union of cosets of some non-zero subgroup of $G$ (i.e., $A$ is periodic). A sum-free subset that is not contained in any induced sum-free subset is called primitive.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture: for every integer $r \geq 1$, if $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_3^r$ is a sum-free subset with
$$|A| > \frac{3^{r-1}+1}{2},$$
then $A$ is contained in an induced sum-free subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^r$.

Equivalently, determine whether the maximum size of a primitive (not contained in any induced) sum-free subset of $\mathbb{F}_3^r$ equals $(3^{r-1}+1)/2$.
artifact.status_search_result: Web search did not find a resolution of this specific conjecture about primitive sum-free subsets in $\mathbb{F}_3^r$. The compilation lists it as an open problem and notes verification only for small $r$ (up to about $r \leq 4$); no later proof or counterexample was located.
